notes.meaning: Benjamin had five main sons listed here: Bela, Ashbel, Aharah, Nohah, and Rapha. The writer returns to Benjamin in greater detail than before because Israel's first king, Saul, came from this tribe, and many Benjamites returned from the Babylonian exile alongside Judah. This list focuses on the sons who founded the major family branches of the tribe.

Bela's sons are listed, including Addar, Gera, Abihud, Abishua, Naaman, Ahoah, Shephuphan, and Huram. Some of these men were grandsons or later clan leaders who were counted as Bela's sons in tribal records. God carefully preserved these family lines even after Benjamin suffered terrible losses in earlier history.

These verses describe the family heads descended from Ehud who lived in Geba and were moved to Manahath. Gera led this relocation, and he was the father of Uzza and Ahihud. Families often had to move to new districts when local numbers grew or when earlier wars disrupted their original towns.

Shaharaim had sons in the land of Moab after he divorced or sent away his wives Hushim and Baara. He probably sought relief in Moab during a time of famine or trouble in Israel, just as Elimelech and Naomi once did. Even when households faced separation and hardship in foreign lands, God did not forget them.

Shaharaim had seven sons by his wife Hodesh in Moab, including Jobab, Mesha, and Malcam. These sons grew to become respected leaders of their own family groups. Their names reflect the Moabite culture around them, showing how living among foreigners influenced their household.

Shaharaim also fathered two sons with Hushim before she was sent away, named Abitub and Elpaal. This branch of the family remained in the promised land rather than staying in Moab. From Elpaal came a large line of future clan leaders and town builders.

Elpaal's sons built the towns of Ono and Lod with their nearby villages. In addition, his descendants Beriah and Shema ruled in Aijalon and drove out Philistine raiders from Gath. God gave these families the courage to rebuild destroyed towns and protect their people from ancient enemies.

Beriah's sons are listed, including Ahio, Shashak, Jeremoth, Zebadiah, and Michael. These men served as heads of their households and maintained their family honor after their victories in battle. Their names were preserved so that later generations would remember their courage.

Seven sons of Elpaal are named, including Zebadiah, Meshullam, Hizki, Heber, Ishmerai, Izliah, and Jobab. These brothers led distinct family units within the tribe of Benjamin. Each leader helped maintain his family's place in Israel's community.

Nine sons of Shimei, also called Shema, are named, including Jakim, Zichri, and Shimrath. They governed household groups in Benjamin's territory. Keeping track of each family branch helped returning exiles reclaim their ancestral inheritances.

Six sons of Shashak are named: Ishpan, Eber, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, and Hanan. They served as heads of their family groups within the tribe. Every family leader had a valued role in strengthening the life of God's people.

Five more sons of Shashak are listed: Hananiah, Elam, Anthothijah, Iphdeiah, and Penuel. Like their brothers, they served as responsible leaders over their households in Benjamin. God honors ordinary parents and leaders who care faithfully for their kin.

Six sons of Jeroham are listed: Shamsherai, Shehariah, Athaliah, Jaareshiah, Elijah, and Zichri. These men led their own family branches under the tribe of Benjamin. Their recorded names gave post-exilic believers clear links back to their ancestors.

This verse summarizes all the family heads listed in the previous verses and notes that they lived in Jerusalem. Settling in Jerusalem after the exile was difficult and dangerous because the city was broken down and surrounded by enemies. Their bravery in choosing God's city set an inspiring example for others to follow.

Jeiel is called the father or ruler of Gibeon, where he lived with his wife Maacah. His firstborn son was Abdon, followed by Zur, Kish, Baal, and Nadab. Gibeon was an important town northwest of Jerusalem where this branch of the tribe established its home.

Jeiel's remaining sons were Gedor, Ahio, Zecher, and Mikloth, who was the father of Shimeah. Unlike most of their relatives who stayed in Gibeon, Shimeah's family chose to live near their fellow Benjamites in Jerusalem. God honors families who step out to support His worshiping community.

Ner was the father of Kish, Kish was the father of King Saul, and Saul had four sons: Jonathan, Malchishua, Abinadab, and Esh-baal. This verse brings the genealogy to Saul, the first king of Israel. Esh-baal was later called Ish-bosheth in 2 Samuel because people avoided using the name Baal once it was tied to idols.

Jonathan had a son named Merib-baal, who became the father of Micah. Merib-baal is known as Mephibosheth in 2 Samuel, where King David showed him great kindness for Jonathan's sake. God preserved Jonathan's royal line through this son because of the covenant of friendship made between David and Jonathan.

Micah had four sons named Pithon, Melech, Tarea, and Ahaz. These sons carried forward the family line long after Saul's earthly dynasty had ended. Even when human kingdoms collapse, God continues to watch over the households of His faithful servants.

Ahaz's line is traced through Jehoaddah, Zimri, Moza, Binea, Raphah, and Eleasah down to Azel. Jonathan's family line survived through many generations right up toward the time of the exile. God remained faithful to preserve this household across several centuries.

Azel had six sons named Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, and Hanan. All six are named as heads of families in this continuing royal line. Their names proved to the returned exiles that Jonathan's descendants had not vanished from the earth.

Azel's brother Eshek had sons whose line grew into a large clan of 150 valiant men and skilled archers under Ulam. These warriors used heavy bows that they bent with their feet and hands, continuing Benjamin's long tradition of military prowess. The chapter closes by celebrating how God raised a small, broken tribe into a thriving and courageous people.
